# B1 on M5: the beer game driven by 70 store-by-department series

*Generated by `run_m5.py` on 19 November 2026. Demand is real M5 unit sales (Walmart, 2011 to 2016), aggregated to weeks. The supply chain is simulated: M5 has sales, not orders or inventory, so nothing here says what Walmart's chain did. The human-like parameters are still **placeholders** (Sterman 1989 could not be read), the DQN (P3) and the forecast inputs (F1, F2) are not part of these runs, and replications R1 to R3 are not passed. Read the result as: how the policy classes compare on this chain and this demand.*

## 1. Data

- Source: the M5 organisers' Google Drive package (`Dataset/sales_train_evaluation.csv`, `Dataset/calendar.csv`), fetched without a login. **The terms of use for redistributing derived aggregates were not found** (neither the ReadMe nor the Competitors Guide pages read state them), so no data file is committed; `prepare_m5.py` rebuilds the aggregates.
- Facts checked against the Competitors Guide (Table 1, section "The dataset"): 42,840 series in total, **70 at the store-by-department level**, 1,941 days of history (29 January 2011 to 19 June 2016), 10 stores, 7 departments. Our file has 70 series of 277 full weeks (the 1,941st day starts an incomplete week, which is dropped). Mean weekly units run from 84 to 20,386; no series has a zero week.
- Scaling: each series is multiplied so its **training** mean is 100 cases a week; the test window played no part in it. Costs are in that scaled unit.

## 2. Design (as frozen in CRITERIA.md)

Tuning on weeks 0 to 224 with cost counted from week 52; test on the last 52 weeks (weeks 225 to 276) with the parameters frozen, the chain replayed from week 0 so its state at the start of the window is real. P1 and P2 use the same search effort (level 2); P1 tunes 4 levels and P2 16 parameters, so P2 searches a larger space. 70 series completed, 0 failed.

## 3. S3: all four stages use the same policy

| policy | median chain cost | IQR | series it is cheapest on | fill rate | Retailer bullwhip (median) | Wholesaler bullwhip (median) | Distributor bullwhip (median) | Factory bullwhip (median) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P0 human-like (placeholder parameters) | 29618 | 24425 to 49686 | 4 of 70 | 0.999 | 1.53 | 4.08 | 12.68 | 31.09 |
| P1 base-stock (formula levels) | 10358 | 7642 to 19319 | 43 of 70 | 0.985 | 1.00 | 0.98 | 0.96 | 0.96 |
| P1 base-stock (tuned) | 16442 | 9131 to 36490 | 11 of 70 | 0.975 | 1.00 | 0.98 | 0.96 | 0.96 |
| P2 SD rule (tuned) | 19676 | 9733 to 41854 | 12 of 70 | 0.956 | 0.84 | 0.77 | 1.25 | 1.65 |

| comparison | median relative cost difference | 90% interval over series | Hodges-Lehmann | share of series the first wins | Wilcoxon p | effect r |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| M5 S3: P2 vs P1 tuned | +1.5% | -36.1% to +97.8% | +5.7% | 0.46 | 0.147 | 0.17 |
| M5 S3: P2 vs P0 (descriptive) | -55.2% | -82.2% to +71.9% | -45.4% | 0.83 | 5.59e-06 | -0.54 |
| M5 S3: P1 tuned vs P1 formula (descriptive) | +58.8% | -52.8% to +363.0% | +59.0% | 0.23 | 1.43e-07 | 0.63 |

**Confirmatory comparison (P2 versus tuned P1, S3, 70 series):** median relative cost difference +1.5%. By the pre-fixed reading: parity (within ±2%): expected when beta is near 1; not evidence of superiority.

**Cost of misperception** ((P2 - P0) / P0, descriptive): -55.2% median. With placeholder human parameters this is not a statement about people.

## 4. S1 and S2 at the retailer position (the other three stages fixed)

| scenario | P2 vs tuned P1: median | 90% interval | share of series P2 wins | Wilcoxon p |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 others base-stock (tuned), Retailer | +0.8% | -10.0% to +26.5% | 0.44 | 0.0706 |
| S2 others human-like, Retailer | -3.5% | -38.0% to +4.3% | 0.77 | 7.77e-08 |

Beta found by tuning at the retailer in S3 (P2): median 1.99, 10th to 90th percentile 0.74 to 2.87 (1 means the supply line is fully counted; the search allowed 0 to 3).

## 5. Checks on the result

- **Bounds:** of 280 tuned betas, 0 sit at the upper bound (3); of 280 tuned thetas, 5 sit at the lower bound (0.05). The largest tuned desired stock is below the bound (15 times the starting demand).
- **The test window is harder than training:** the P2 cost over the last 52 weeks is a median 1.95 times the training cost per 52 weeks, because the last year has more demand and variation. This applies to every policy, so the comparison is unaffected, but absolute costs are not comparable between windows.
- **Leakage:** the scaling uses the training weeks only; the tuning runs end at week 225 and integrate only weeks 0 to 224; the test run replays the same series with the parameters frozen. P1's tuned levels and P2's parameters never saw a test week.
- **Reading across the pilot:** on synthetic i.i.d. demand the tuned SD rule beat tuned base-stock by about 12 to 18%; on the real series the two are level. The edge in the pilot depended on demand with no trend or seasonality.

## 6. What this does and does not show

- It shows how a tuned base-stock rule, a tuned order-smoothing SD rule and a placeholder human-like rule compare on 70 real demand series in one simulated chain, with parameters fixed before the test window.
- It does not show that the SD rule is better than the optimum: echelon base-stock, the DQN and forecast-driven policies were not run.
- Demand at this level is smooth and has weekly and yearly seasonality; the result does not carry to item-store daily ordering.
- The parameters were tuned per series on 225 weeks of that series' own history, which is a luxury a real planner may not have.

This run took 54 seconds. Reproduce: `python3 prepare_m5.py && python3 build_model.py && python3 run_m5.py`.
